{{Short description|Concept in combinatorics (part of mathematics)}}
{{DISPLAYTITLE:''q''-Pochhammer symbol}}
In the [[mathematics|mathematical]] field of [[combinatorics]], the '''''q''-Pochhammer symbol''', also called the '''''q''-shifted factorial''', is the product
<math display="block">(a;q)_n = \prod_{k=0}^{n-1} (1-aq^k)=(1-a)(1-aq)(1-aq^2)\cdots(1-aq^{n-1}),</math>
with <math>(a;q)_0 = 1.</math>
It is a [[q-analog|''q''-analog]] of the [[Pochhammer symbol]] <math>x^{(n)} = x(x+1)\dots(x+n-1)</math>, in the sense that
<math display="block">\lim_{q\to1} \frac{(q^x;q)_n}{(1-q)^n} = x^{(n)}.</math>
The ''q''-Pochhammer symbol is a major building block in the construction of ''q''-analogs; for instance, in the theory of [[basic hypergeometric series]], it plays the role that the ordinary Pochhammer symbol plays in the theory of [[generalized hypergeometric series]].

Unlike the ordinary Pochhammer symbol, the ''q''-Pochhammer symbol can be extended to an [[infinite product]]:
<math display="block">(a;q)_\infty = \prod_{k=0}^{\infty} (1-aq^k).</math>
This is an [[analytic function]] of ''q'' in the interior of the [[unit disk]], and can also be considered as a [[formal power series]] in ''q''.  The special case
<math display="block">\phi(q) = (q;q)_\infty=\prod_{k=1}^\infty (1-q^k)</math>
is known as [[Euler's function]], and is important in [[combinatorics]], [[number theory]], and the theory of [[modular forms]].

==Identities==
The finite product can be expressed in terms of the infinite product:
<math display="block">(a;q)_n = \frac{(a;q)_\infty} {(aq^n;q)_\infty}, </math>
which extends the definition to negative integers ''n''.  Thus, for nonnegative ''n'', one has
<math display="block">(a;q)_{-n} = \frac{1}{(aq^{-n};q)_n}=\prod_{k=1}^n \frac{1}{(1-a/q^k)}</math>
and
<math display="block">(a;q)_{-n} = \frac{(-q/a)^n q^{n(n-1)/2}} {(q/a;q)_n}.</math>
Alternatively,
<math display="block">\prod_{k=n}^\infty (1-aq^k)=(aq^n;q)_\infty = \frac{(a;q)_\infty} {(a;q)_n}, </math>
which is useful for some of the generating functions of partition functions.

The ''q''-Pochhammer symbol is the subject of a number of ''q''-series identities, particularly the infinite series expansions
<math display="block">(x;q)_\infty = \sum_{n=0}^\infty \frac{(-1)^n q^{n(n-1)/2}}{(q;q)_n} x^n</math>
and
<math display="block">\frac{1}{(x;q)_\infty}=\sum_{n=0}^\infty \frac{x^n}{(q;q)_n},</math>
which are both special cases of the [[q-binomial theorem|''q''-binomial theorem]]:
<math display="block">\frac{(ax;q)_\infty}{(x;q)_\infty} = \sum_{n=0}^\infty \frac{(a;q)_n}{(q;q)_n} x^n.</math>
[[Fridrikh Karpelevich]] found the following identity (see {{harvs|txt|last1=Olshanetsky|last2=Rogov|year=1995}} for the proof):
<math display="block">\frac{(q;q)_{\infty}}{(z;q)_{\infty}}=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{(-1)^{n}q^{n(n+1)/2}}{(q;q)_n(1-zq^{n})}, \ |z|<1.</math>

==Combinatorial interpretation==

The ''q''-Pochhammer symbol is closely related to the [[enumerative combinatorics]] of partitions. The coefficient of <math>q^m a^n</math> in
<math display="block">(a;q)_\infty^{-1} = \prod_{k=0}^{\infty} (1-aq^k)^{-1}</math>
is the number of partitions of ''m'' into at most ''n'' parts.
Since, by conjugation of partitions, this is the same as the number of partitions of ''m'' into parts of size at most ''n'', by identification of generating series we obtain the identity
<math display="block">(a;q)_\infty^{-1} = \sum_{k=0}^\infty \left(\prod_{j=1}^k \frac{1}{1-q^j} \right) a^k
                         = \sum_{k=0}^\infty \frac{a^k}{(q;q)_k}</math>
as in the above section.

We also have that the coefficient of <math>q^m a^n</math> in
<math display="block">(-a;q)_\infty = \prod_{k=0}^{\infty} (1+aq^k)</math>
is the number of partitions of ''m'' into ''n'' or ''n''-1 distinct parts.

By removing a triangular partition with ''n'' − 1 parts from such a partition, we are left with an arbitrary partition with at most ''n'' parts. This gives a weight-preserving [[bijection]] between the set of partitions into ''n'' or ''n'' − 1 distinct parts and the set of pairs consisting of a triangular partition having ''n'' − 1 parts and a partition with at most ''n'' parts. By identifying generating series, this leads to the identity
<math display="block">(-a;q)_\infty = \prod_{k=0}^\infty (1+aq^k)
                     = \sum_{k=0}^\infty \left(q^{k\choose 2} \prod_{j=1}^k \frac{1}{1-q^j}\right) a^k
                     = \sum_{k=0}^\infty \frac{q^{k\choose 2}}{(q;q)_k} a^k</math>
also described in the above section. 
The reciprocal of the function <math>(q)_{\infty} := (q; q)_{\infty}</math> similarly arises as the [[generating function]] for the [[partition function (number theory)|partition function]], <math>p(n)</math>, which is also expanded by the second two [[q-series]] expansions given below:<ref>{{cite web|last1=Berndt|first1=B. C.|title=What is a q-series?|url=http://www.math.uiuc.edu/~berndt/articles/q.pdf}}</ref>
<math display="block">\frac{1}{(q; q)_{\infty}} = \sum_{n \geq 0} p(n) q^n = \sum_{n \geq 0} \frac{q^n}{(q; q)_n} = \sum_{n \geq 0} \frac{q^{n^2}}{(q; q)_n^2}. </math>

The [[q-binomial theorem|''q''-binomial theorem]] itself can also be handled by a slightly more involved combinatorial argument of a similar flavor (see also the expansions given in the [[Q-Pochhammer symbol#Relationship to other q-functions|next subsection]]).

Similarly,
<math display="block">(q; q)_{\infty} = 1 - \sum_{n \geq 0} q^{n+1}(q; q)_n = \sum_{n \geq 0} q^{\frac{n(n+1)}{2}}\frac{(-1)^n}{(q; q)_n}.</math>

== Multiple arguments convention ==

Since identities involving ''q''-Pochhammer symbols so frequently involve products of many symbols, the standard convention is to write a product as a single symbol of multiple arguments:
<math display="block">(a_1,a_2,\ldots,a_m;q)_n = (a_1;q)_n (a_2;q)_n \ldots (a_m;q)_n.</math>

== ''q''-series ==
{{main|q-analog}}
{{Redirect|q-series|other uses|Q series (disambiguation)}}
A ''q''-series is a [[Series (mathematics)|series]] in which the coefficients are functions of ''q'', typically expressions of <math>(a; q)_{n}</math>.<ref>Bruce C. Berndt, [http://www.math.uiuc.edu/~berndt/articles/q.pdf What is a ''q''-series?], in Ramanujan Rediscovered: Proceedings of a Conference on Elliptic Functions, Partitions, and q-Series in memory of K. Venkatachaliengar: Bangalore, 1–5 June 2009, N. D. Baruah, B. C. Berndt, S. Cooper, T. Huber, and M. J. Schlosser, eds., Ramanujan Mathematical Society, Mysore, 2010, pp. 31–51.</ref> Early results are due to [[Euler]], [[Gauss]], and [[Cauchy]]. The systematic study begins with [[Eduard Heine]] (1843).<ref>{{cite web|last1=Heine|first1=E.|title=Untersuchungen über die Reihe|url=https://gdz.sub.uni-goettingen.de/id/PPN243919689_0034?tify=%7B%22view%22%3A%22info%22%2C%22pages%22%3A%5B299%5D%7D}} J. Reine Angew. Math. 34 (1847), 285–328.</ref>

== Relationship to other ''q''-functions ==

The ''q''-analog of ''n'', also known as the '''''q''-bracket''' or '''''q''-number''' of ''n'', is defined to be
<math display="block">[n]_q=\frac{1-q^n}{1-q}.</math>
From this one can define the ''q''-analog of the [[factorial]], the '''''q''-factorial''', as

<math display="block">
\begin{align}
\left[n\right]!_q & = \prod_{k=1}^n [k]_q = [1]_q \cdot [2]_q \cdots [n-1]_q \cdot [n]_q \\
& = \frac{1-q}{1-q} \frac{1-q^2}{1-q} \cdots \frac{1-q^{n-1}}{1-q} \frac{1-q^n}{1-q} \\
& = 1 \cdot (1+q)\cdots (1+q+\cdots + q^{n-2}) \cdot (1+q+\cdots + q^{n-1}) \\
& = \frac{(q;q)_n}{(1-q)^n} \\
\end{align}
</math>

These numbers are analogues in the sense that  
<math display="block">\lim_{q\rightarrow 1}[n]_q = n,</math>
and so also 
<math display="block">\lim_{q\rightarrow 1}[n]!_q = n!.</math>

The limit value ''n''! counts [[permutation]]s of an ''n''-element set ''S''.  Equivalently, it counts the number of sequences of nested sets <math>E_1 \subset E_2 \subset \cdots \subset E_n = S</math> such that <math>E_i</math> contains exactly ''i'' elements.<ref name="EC1">{{citation | last = Stanley | first = Richard P. | authorlink = Richard P. Stanley | title = Enumerative Combinatorics | volume = 1 | edition = 2 | publisher = Cambridge University Press | year = 2011}}, Section 1.10.2.</ref>  By comparison, when ''q'' is a [[prime power]] and ''V'' is an ''n''-dimensional [[vector space]] over the field with ''q'' elements, the ''q''-analogue <math>[n]!_q</math> is the number of [[complete flag]]s in ''V'', that is, it is the number of sequences <math>V_1 \subset V_2 \subset \cdots \subset V_n = V</math> of subspaces such that <math>V_i</math> has dimension ''i''.<ref name = "EC1" />  The preceding considerations suggest that one can regard a sequence of nested sets as a flag over a conjectural [[field with one element]].

A product of negative [[integer]] ''q''-brackets can be expressed in terms of the ''q''-factorial as
<math display="block">\prod_{k=1}^n [-k]_q = \frac{(-1)^n\,[n]!_q}{q^{n(n+1)/2}}</math>

From the ''q''-factorials, one can move on to define the ''q''-binomial coefficients, also known as the [[Gaussian binomial coefficient]]s, as
<math display="block">
\begin{bmatrix}
n\\
k
\end{bmatrix}_q
=
\frac{[n]!_q}{[n-k]!_q [k]!_q}, 
</math>

where it is easy to see that the triangle of these coefficients is symmetric in the sense that

:<math>\begin{bmatrix} n \\ m \end{bmatrix}_q = \begin{bmatrix} n \\ n-m \end{bmatrix}_q</math>

for all <math>0 \leq m \leq n</math>. One can check that

<math display="block">
\begin{align}
\begin{bmatrix}
n+1\\
k
\end{bmatrix}_q
 & =
\begin{bmatrix}
n\\
k
\end{bmatrix}_q
+
q^{n-k+1}
\begin{bmatrix}
n\\
k-1
\end{bmatrix}_q \\ 
 & = 
\begin{bmatrix} n \\ k-1 \end{bmatrix}_q + q^k \begin{bmatrix} n \\ k \end{bmatrix}_q.
\end{align}
</math>

One can also see from the previous recurrence relations that the next variants of the <math>q</math>-binomial theorem are expanded in terms of these coefficients as follows:<ref>{{cite book|last1=Olver |display-authors=et al.|title=NIST Handbook of Mathematical Functions|date=2010|section=Section 17.2|page=421|url=http://dlmf.nist.gov/}}</ref>
<math display="block">
\begin{align} 
(z; q)_n & = \sum_{j=0}^n \begin{bmatrix} n \\ j \end{bmatrix}_q (-z)^j q^{\binom{j}{2}} = (1-z)(1-qz) \cdots (1-z q^{n-1}) \\ 
(-q; q)_n & = \sum_{j=0}^n \begin{bmatrix} n \\ j \end{bmatrix}_{q^2} q^j \\ 
(q; q^2)_n & = \sum_{j=0}^{2n} \begin{bmatrix} 2n \\ j \end{bmatrix}_q (-1)^j \\ 
\frac{1}{(z; q)_{m+1}} & = \sum_{n \geq 0} \begin{bmatrix} n+m \\ n \end{bmatrix}_q z^n. 
\end{align}
</math>

One may further define the ''q''-multinomial coefficients
<math display="block">
\begin{bmatrix}
n\\
k_1, \ldots ,k_m
\end{bmatrix}_q
=
\frac{[n]!_q}{[k_1]!_q \cdots [k_m]!_q}, 
</math>
where the arguments <math>k_1, \ldots, k_m</math> are nonnegative integers that satisfy <math>
\sum_{i=1}^m k_i = n 
</math>. The coefficient above counts the number of flags
<math>
V_1 \subset  \dots \subset V_m
</math> 
of subspaces in an ''n''-dimensional vector space over the field with ''q'' elements such that <math>
\dim V_i = \sum_{j=1}^i k_j
</math>.

The limit <math>q\to 1</math> gives the usual multinomial coefficient <math>{n\choose k_1,\dots ,k_m}</math>, which counts words in ''n'' different symbols <math>\{s_1,\dots,s_m\}</math> such that each <math>s_i</math> appears <math>k_i</math> times. 

One also obtains a ''q''-analog of the [[gamma function]], called the '''[[q-gamma function]]''', and defined as
<math display="block">\Gamma_q(x)=\frac{(1-q)^{1-x} (q;q)_\infty}{(q^x;q)_\infty}</math>
This converges to the usual gamma function as ''q'' approaches 1 from inside the unit disc. Note that
<math display="block">\Gamma_q(x+1)=[x]_q\Gamma_q(x)</math>
for any ''x'' and
<math display="block">\Gamma_q(n+1)=[n]!_q</math>
for non-negative integer values of ''n''. Alternatively, this may be taken as an extension of the ''q''-factorial function to the [[real number]] system.
